Most of the negatively correlated pairs of periodontitis-decreased genera involve *Oribacterium*, which is only weakly supported as decreased in periodontitis (`r perio_genera$decreased[perio_genera$taxon == "Oribacterium"]` of `r perio_genera$signatures[perio_genera$taxon == "Oribacterium"]` signatures) and in healthy plaque correlates with the periodontitis-increased genera. The Human Microbiome Project screened its participants for oral health, so this variation exists without diagnosed periodontitis, though it may include mild gingival inflammation.

### Agreement across approaches

```{r method-agreement}
# conditions passing FDR < 0.05 in the same direction as periodontitis, by approach
fdr_hits <- \(d) paste(sort(unique(d$Condition)), collapse = ", ")
method_agreement <- tribble(
  ~Approach, ~`Compared with`, ~Conditions,
  "Genus enrichment", "all BugSigDB studies",
  fdr_hits(filter(bind_rows(enrichment_table("increased"), enrichment_table("decreased")), fdr < 0.05)),
  "Genus enrichment", "same body site group",
  fdr_hits(filter(bind_rows(enrichment_table("increased", match_site = TRUE),
                            enrichment_table("decreased", match_site = TRUE)), fdr < 0.05)),
  "Genus direction", "50% (no direction preference)",
  fdr_hits(filter(bind_rows(direction_tests("increased"), direction_tests("decreased")), fdr < 0.05, same / n > 0.5)),
  "Whole-signature similarity", "all BugSigDB study units",
  fdr_hits(filter(semsim_all$stats, fdr < 0.05, perio == direction)),
  "Whole-signature similarity", "same body site group",
  fdr_hits(filter(semsim_site$stats, fdr < 0.05, perio == direction)),
  "Jaccard genus overlap", "all BugSigDB study units",
  fdr_hits(filter(jaccard_tests$all, fdr < 0.05, perio == direction)),
  "Jaccard genus overlap", "same body site group",
  fdr_hits(filter(jaccard_tests$site, fdr < 0.05, perio == direction))
)
kbl(method_agreement, caption = "Conditions significantly similar to periodontitis (FDR < 0.05, same direction as periodontitis) in each literature-based approach.") |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Table details
- **What a row lists**: conditions with at least one FDR < 0.05 result in the same direction as periodontitis in that approach. For genus approaches, that means any of the 20 top genera in that direction.
- **Genus enrichment, all studies**: one-sided Fisher's exact test of the share of the condition's study units with the genus vs all other units of that direction (conditions with ≥5 units). BH across all genus × condition tests per direction.
- **Genus enrichment, same body site group**: the same test, but one-sided exact Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel stratified by body site group.
- **Genus direction**: two-sided binomial test of a condition's units reporting the genus increased vs decreased; listed only if FDR < 0.05 and the majority is in the periodontitis direction.
- **Whole-signature similarity / Jaccard**: one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test of the condition's study-unit similarity ranks against 0.5, with BH within each column. The ranks are among all units of that direction, or within the same body site group. Jaccard compares genera only, with the consensus taxa mapped to genus.
- **Reading**: only colorectal cancer survives all seven. The four other conditions listed without site matching (COVID-19, head and neck cancer, rheumatoid arthritis, smoking) mostly drop out once compared within the same body site group.
:::

Colorectal cancer showed the most consistent overlap with periodontitis-associated taxa across the literature-based comparisons: it is the only condition flagged by every approach, and its overlap remained significant after BH correction in the body-site-stratified genus enrichment and both taxonomic-similarity analyses. Increases in *Fusobacterium*, *Parvimonas*, *Peptostreptococcus* and *Porphyromonas* were disproportionately reported in colorectal cancer studies, and whole-signature similarity supports the overlap using taxa at their reported taxonomic ranks. Results for other conditions were less consistent across methods: several oral conditions pass before body site stratification but not after it, and rheumatoid arthritis also shows significant genus overlap in the body-site-matched Jaccard analysis.

In colorectal cancer stool datasets, the periodontitis-increased signature frequently ranked highly, although statistical support varied by dataset and enrichment method; no periodontitis signature passed FDR with PADOG. The periodontitis-decreased signature did not show corresponding evidence.

```{r bsdb-robustness}
# is colorectal cancer singled out because it is one of the largest conditions?
set.seed(1)
inc_sigs <- filter(bsdb_sigs, direction == "increased")
core <- c("Fusobacterium", "Parvimonas", "Peptostreptococcus", "Porphyromonas")
core_hits <- bsdb_genera |> filter(direction == "increased", taxon %in% core) |> distinct(sig, taxon)
large <- inc_sigs |> count(Condition, sort = TRUE) |> slice_head(n = 4)
large_oe <- site_expected(inc_sigs, core_hits) |>
  filter(Condition %in% large$Condition) |>
  summarise(max_ratio = max(observed / expected), .by = Condition)
large_sim <- semsim_site$stats |> filter(direction == "increased", perio == "increased", Condition %in% large$Condition)
others <- setdiff(large$Condition, "Colorectal cancer")
others_sim <- paste(sprintf("%s %.2f", others, large_sim$mean_rank[match(others, large_sim$Condition)]), collapse = ", ")

# subsample colorectal cancer to 15 study units
crc_sigs <- filter(inc_sigs, Condition == "Colorectal cancer")
sub_enrich <- replicate(200, {
  keep <- sample(crc_sigs$sig, 15)
  s2 <- filter(inc_sigs, Condition != "Colorectal cancer" | sig %in% keep)
  sapply(core, \(g) site_matched_p("Colorectal cancer", g, s2, core_hits)) < 0.05
})
crc_ranks <- semsim_site$units |> filter(Condition == "Colorectal cancer", direction == "increased", perio == "increased") |> pull(rank)
sub_sim <- replicate(1000, wilcox.test(sample(crc_ranks, 15), mu = 0.5, alternative = "greater", exact = FALSE)$p.value < 0.05)
pct <- \(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Robustness details
- **Largest conditions**: by number of increased study units: Parkinson's disease 59, colorectal cancer 54, COVID-19 42, obesity 39.
- **Observed ÷ expected**: share of the condition's units reporting each of *Fusobacterium*, *Parvimonas*, *Peptostreptococcus* and *Porphyromonas* increased ÷ the share in other conditions from the same body site groups, weighted by the condition's site mix. Colorectal cancer: up to 13.3× (e.g. *Parvimonas* 0.41 vs 0.03 expected). The other three: at most 1.09×.
- **Similarity ranks** (to the periodontitis-increased consensus, within site group; 0.5 = typical): colorectal cancer 0.72 (FDR 0.0008), COVID-19 0.43, obesity 0.51, Parkinson's 0.34.
- **Subsampling enrichment**: 200 draws of 15 of colorectal cancer's 54 increased units. Each genus is re-tested with the one-sided site-stratified exact test, unadjusted p < 0.05. Significant in 97% (*Porphyromonas*) to 100% (*Parvimonas*, *Peptostreptococcus*) of draws.
- **Subsampling similarity**: 1,000 draws of 15 of its 47 rank values, one-sided Wilcoxon test against 0.5, p < 0.05 in 82% of draws.
- **Watch out**: subsampling keeps the other conditions fixed and uses unadjusted p, so it shows the signal is not just a sample-size effect, not that it would pass FDR at n = 15.
:::

**Robustness:** colorectal cancer is not singled out simply because it is one of the largest conditions in BugSigDB. The other largest conditions (`r paste(others, collapse = ", ")`) show none of the signal: none reports any of *Fusobacterium*, *Parvimonas*, *Peptostreptococcus* or *Porphyromonas* more than `r sprintf("%.1f", max(large_oe$max_ratio[large_oe$Condition != "Colorectal cancer"]))` times as often as expected, and their similarity ranks to the periodontitis-increased signature are `r others_sim` (0.5 = typical). When colorectal cancer is cut to 15 random study units, the size of a typical condition, the four genera stay significantly enriched in `r pct(min(rowMeans(sub_enrich)))`–`r pct(max(rowMeans(sub_enrich)))` of draws and the similarity in `r pct(mean(sub_sim))`.

# Summary and limitations

PerioSigDB contains substantial variation in comparison-group definitions, participant characteristics, clinical measurements and profiling methods. Metadata availability is uneven, particularly for systemic health status and several clinical measures. Periodontitis-increased signatures show greater between-study similarity than random oral signatures, and colorectal cancer is the condition whose literature overlaps most consistently with them.

These findings describe shared microbial associations. They do not show a causal relationship between periodontitis and colorectal cancer, bacterial transfer between body sites, or diagnostic performance. Limitations:

- **Assay coverage:** about half of PerioSigDB signatures come from targeted assays, so reporting frequencies partly reflect which taxa were measured.
- **Sampling sites:** body site groups are broad; PerioSigDB is subgingival plaque, while BugSigDB oral studies include saliva, tongue and other sites.
- **Taxonomic resolution:** aggregating species to genus loses specificity (e.g. *P. gingivalis* increased, *P. catoniae* decreased).
- **Metadata:** incomplete, and "not reported" can mean "not entered".
- **Independence:** studies and datasets are treated as independent, although some share cohorts or authors.
- **Comparisons:** the BugSigDB disease-vs-control filter works on group names, and comparison groups in PerioSigDB include some participants with gingivitis and periodontitis-resistant older adults.

- Thomas AM, Manghi P, Asnicar F, et al. Metagenomic analysis of colorectal cancer datasets identifies cross-cohort microbial diagnostic signatures and a link with choline degradation. *Nat Med*. 2019;25(4):667–678.
- Wirbel J, Pyl PT, Kartal E, et al. Meta-analysis of fecal metagenomes reveals global microbial signatures that are specific for colorectal cancer. *Nat Med*. 2019;25(4):679–689.
